prime.problem: Merge sort, binary search, quickselect and the median cut all split a problem and recurse, yet their costs are n log n, log n, n and log n. Without a rule, every recursive algorithm needs its own ad-hoc analysis, and you can't tell in advance whether a new split will pay off.
prime.fits: The first Paradigms card brings the course's recursive algorithms back under one lens: merge sort, quickselect, binary search and the median of two arrays, plus Karatsuba as a new example where cutting the number of calls is the whole win.
expect: leaves n^(log_b a) vs top-level work f(n)
three cases: leaves win, tie, root wins
prime.goal: Read a recurrence, identify a, b and f, pick the master-theorem case, and explain from the per-level work why that case gives that answer.

attend: Why does the recursion tree have n^(log_b a) leaves, and why is that the number to compare f(n) against?
In the level table for n = 1,024, why is merge sort's column constant, Karatsuba's growing and quickselect's shrinking?
Why does splitting a multiply into four half-size products buy nothing, while three does?
Why doesn't the theorem apply to worst-case quicksort's T(n − 1) + n?
When do overlapping subproblems turn divide and conquer into dynamic programming?

must: Level i has aⁱ calls of size n/bⁱ → work per level aⁱ·f(n/bⁱ) → the total is dominated by whichever end of the tree is biggest → compare f(n) with the leaf count n^(log_b a)

Leaves win (f smaller) → Θ(n^(log_b a)), e.g. Karatsuba 3T(n/2) + n → n^1.585; tie (equal) → every level costs the same → Θ(n^(log_b a) log n), e.g. merge sort n log n, binary search log n; root wins (f bigger, regular) → Θ(f(n)), e.g. quickselect's expected n
Leaves = n^(log_b a) depend on a, not on how clever the split is → four half-products still give n² → cutting a to 3 gives 3¹⁰ = 59,049 vs 4¹⁰ = 1,048,576 one-digit products at 1,024 digits (17.76×)
elevated: The theorem needs equal pieces n/b and a polynomial gap between f and the leaves → T(n − 1) + n, T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n and 2T(n/2) + n / log n fall outside → unroll, draw the recursion tree, or use Akra–Bazzi
reference: the regularity condition's exact form a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw one recursion tree with the per-level work written beside each level, then write the three cases as "which end of the tree wins → answer" with one algorithm from this course for each.
checklist: T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n); leaves n^(log_b a)
tie → times log n (merge sort, binary search)
outside the theorem: unequal pieces, n − 1 pieces, gaps between cases

retrieve.q: Explain, without the formula, why Karatsuba's three recursive calls make it asymptotically faster while merge sort's two calls make it n log n.
answer: each level multiplies the number of calls by a and halves their size
with a = 3 the calls grow faster than the work per call shrinks, so the leaves dominate: n^(log₂ 3)
with a = 2 and f = n, calls double and sizes halve: every level costs n, so levels × n = n log n

retrieve.q: Walk through the level table for quickselect at n = 1,024: the work at levels 0, 1 and 10, the total, and why it's case 3.
answer: a = 1, b = 2, f = n: level i costs 1024/2ⁱ
the root's n dominates: the series is geometric, so the total is a constant times the top level

retrieve.q: Multiplying two 400-digit numbers in Python: does Karatsuba beat schoolbook here? What does the card say about where the crossover sits and why?
answer: CPython only switches to Karatsuba above 70 internal digits (≈ 632 decimal digits)
400 digits is below that, so schoolbook is used
Karatsuba's extra additions, subtractions and recursion overhead outweigh saving one product in four at small sizes

compare.q: Merge sort's card counts ⌈log₂ n⌉ passes × n; this card calls it case 2. What do the two views agree on, and what does the master theorem let you do that pass-counting doesn't?
answer: both see n work per level and log₂ n levels
pass-counting needs the per-level work to be constant
the theorem also handles levels that grow (Karatsuba) or shrink (quickselect) geometrically

compare.q: Naive Fibonacci splits into two subproblems, like merge sort. Why is merge sort efficient and naive Fibonacci exponential, and what fixes Fibonacci?
answer: merge sort's halves are disjoint, so no work repeats
Fibonacci's T(n − 1) and T(n − 2) overlap heavily: the same subproblems are solved again and again
memoise or tabulate them: that's dynamic programming, O(n)

predict.q: Before computing: which grows faster for large n, 4T(n/2) + n or 2T(n/2) + n²? Commit, then check with the level table at n = 16.
predict.answer: They tie: both are Θ(n²), from opposite ends. 4T(n/2) + n has leaves n² that dominate (levels 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 → total 496). 2T(n/2) + n² has a root n² that dominates (levels 256, 128, 64, 32, 16 → also 496). Same total, mirrored columns.

apply.task: For each recurrence write a, b, f, the leaf count and the case: (1) 3T(n/2) + n, (2) 2T(n/2) + n, (3) 4T(n/2) + n, (4) 2T(n/2) + n². Then fill the per-level work for n = 16 (levels 0–4, base T(1) = f(1)) and total each column.
apply.done: Cases: (1) case 1, n^1.585; (2) case 2, n log n; (3) case 1, n²; (4) case 3, n². Totals at n = 16: 211, 80, 496, 496. The 211 checks against 3·3⁴ − 2·2⁴ = 243 − 32.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: that the two n² recurrences tie, or from which end each gets its n²?
Could you explain case 2's extra log factor from the tree, not the formula?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: a → number of leaves, or f vs leaves → which case?
Which algorithm from this course would you now analyse differently?
What will you look for in the greedy cards: an algorithm that doesn't split at all, and what makes it correct?
